title: What are network effects, and how do you handle a platform case?
description: Why platforms like marketplaces and social networks behave differently, what network effects are, and how to structure a platform case.
hook: A network effect is when a product becomes more valuable to each user as more people use it, as with messaging apps, marketplaces and ride-hailing. To handle a platform case, look at both sides of the market, think locally, judge whether early subsidies will buy a self-sustaining network, and check that the platform's cut (the take rate) leaves both sides happy and still makes money once the network is mature.
body:
What a network effect is

One phone is useless; a phone network everyone uses is invaluable. That is a same-side network effect: users attract more users of the same kind, as in messaging apps and social networks. Many platforms have a cross-side effect instead: two groups who need each other, such as riders and drivers, diners and restaurants, buyers and sellers. More drivers mean shorter waits, which attract more riders, which attract more drivers.

That loop is powerful once it spins, but hard to start, because neither side wants to join an empty platform. This is the chicken-and-egg problem, and most platform launch cases are really about how to solve it.

Network effects are not the same as scale

A warehouse retailer gets cheaper per order as it grows, because it spreads fixed costs. That is an economy of scale, not a network effect: one more customer does not make the service better for the others. Mixing the two up leads to weak answers. Network effects also have limits:

  • They are often local. A ride-hailing app's network effect works within a city. Being big in London does little for a launch in Leeds.
  • They saturate. Once waits are short, more drivers add little for riders but cut each driver's earnings.
  • Users can multi-home. If drivers and riders use two apps at once, neither platform's network is much of a moat.
  • Users can leave the platform. Once a buyer has found a good freelancer, they may pay them directly next time.

What this means in a case

  • Always look at both sides. A drop in orders on a delivery app might be a restaurant problem (fewer good restaurants) rather than a customer problem.
  • Measure liquidity. The share of searches or requests that end in a transaction, and how fast, tells you whether the network is working.
  • Subsidies make sense early, to start the loop, but should shrink as the network grows. If they cannot shrink, the network effect is weaker than claimed.
  • Watch the take rate. It must be low enough that both sides stay, and high enough to make money.

A worked example: the economics of one trip

An illustrative ride costs the passenger $20 and the platform keeps 25%, so $5. Insurance, payments and support cost $2.50 a trip.

  • Mature city: $5 − $2.50 = $2.50 per trip.
  • New city, with a $2 driver bonus per trip: $5 − $2 − $2.50 = $0.50.
  • New city, adding a $1.50 rider discount too: $5 − $2 − $1.50 − $2.50 = −$1.00 per trip.

If launch takes six months at 200,000 trips a month, the platform loses 200,000 × $1.00 × 6 = $1.2M. If the city then settles at 300,000 trips a month with no subsidies, it earns 300,000 × $2.50 = $750k a month, recovering the launch losses in about 1.6 months. The investment is sensible, if the subsidies really can stop without riders and drivers leaving. That is the assumption to test.

A structure for "Should we launch our platform in a new city?"

  • Demand side: how many potential customers, how often they would use it.
  • Supply side: how many drivers, restaurants or sellers we can sign up, and at what cost.
  • Getting to critical mass: subsidies needed and for how long; start narrow (one district, one category) to reach liquidity faster.
  • Competition: is there already a strong local platform, and do users multi-home?
  • Mature unit economics: profit per order or trip once subsidies end.

What a strong answer sounds like

Weak: "The platform has network effects, so the biggest player will win. We should spend whatever it takes to grow."
Strong: "The network effect here is local, so we need to win city by city. I'd check how long subsidies are needed to reach short wait times, and whether drivers also work for the rival app, because if they do, our lead won't stick."

Common mistakes

  • Looking at one side. Every metric should be checked from both sides.
  • Treating user count as proof. A big user base with low repeat use or poor match rates is not a strong network.
  • Assuming winner takes all. Local markets, saturation and multi-homing often leave room for two or more players.
  • Forgetting the end state. Launch losses only make sense if mature unit economics are positive.

Practise

1. A freelance marketplace takes 10% of $200M of jobs a year. It wants to raise its take rate to 12%. How far can job value fall before revenue drops?

Show the answer

Revenue today: $20M. At 12%, it keeps $20M if job value is $20M ÷ 12% ≈ $166.7M, so job value can fall about 16.7%. The risk is a spiral: sellers leave or take clients off the platform, which makes it less useful for buyers, so value falls further.

2. Network effect or economy of scale? (a) A messaging app. (b) A supermarket chain buying more cheaply as it grows. (c) A holiday-rental marketplace.

Show the answer

(a) Same-side network effect: more users make it more useful. (b) Economy of scale: other shoppers do not make the store better for you. (c) Cross-side network effect: more listings attract more guests and vice versa, mostly within each destination.

3. A delivery app earns a 20% commission on $30 orders and pays $3 per order for couriers and support. In a new city it offers customers $1.50 off each order. What is contribution per order, and what must happen for the city to make money?

Show the answer

Commission: $30 × 20% = $6. Contribution: $6 − $3 − $1.50 = $1.50, positive even with the discount. To cover the city's fixed costs it needs enough orders, and it should remove the discount once restaurant choice and delivery times keep customers coming back on their own.

Where to practise next

Try the Hearthstay case (which city should a holiday-rental marketplace launch next), the Patchwork case (raising a marketplace's take rate) and the Palletpoint case (a freight marketplace struggling after launch). For how platforms fit among other business models, see how businesses make money.
